label: Polyhedral Convex Sets And Functions
notes: Open by making finiteness the theme. A polyhedral set has an external finite description by inequalities, while the same set can have an internal finite description by vertices and recession directions. The lecture will keep those two views connected, then lift the same dictionary to functions through epigraphs.

label: Halfspace Intersection
notes: Start with the H-representation because it is the most checkable form. A point belongs to the polyhedron exactly when every affine inequality has nonpositive residual. Equations are not a separate species here, since each equality is just two weak inequalities.

label: Generator Representation
notes: Switch to the internal representation. Vertices describe bounded choices, while directions describe how the set can recede without leaving itself. In the unbounded example, a triangle is swept along one horizontal recession ray, which is why the V-representation uses both a convex hull and a cone.

label: Weyl-Minkowski Dictionary
notes: State the core dictionary as the meeting point of the section: finite halfspaces, finitely many faces, and finite generators describe the same closed convex geometry. The proof route in the source uses faces, so the next slides slow down active inequalities and face structure before returning to computation.

label: Active Constraints
notes: Use the highlighted edge to explain active inequalities. On the relative interior of a face, the active set is stable. At a vertex, more constraints become active. This is the computational version of the face language: face membership can be read from equality residuals.

label: Faces Of Polyhedra
notes: Connect active patterns to the finiteness of faces. A finite inequality list gives only finitely many possible equality patterns, and the relative interiors of faces do not overlap. Vertices, facets, and recession rays are therefore not isolated facts; they are the visible pieces of one finite face structure.

label: Polyhedral Cones
notes: Specialize the dictionary to cones. On the H-side, every boundary hyperplane passes through the origin, so the inequalities are homogeneous. On the V-side, there are no vertices to convex-average; the whole cone is built from nonnegative combinations of finitely many rays.

label: Piecewise-Linear Convex Functions
notes: Move from sets to functions by looking at epigraphs. A proper polyhedral convex function can be read as a finite maximum of affine pieces, possibly restricted to a polyhedral domain by an indicator term. This is the function version of finite inequalities.

label: Epigraph As Polyhedron
notes: Translate the maximum formula into epigraph inequalities. The condition t greater than or equal to every affine piece is a finite system of halfspaces in the lifted space. The lower envelope of those halfspaces is the graph, and the region above it is the epigraph.

label: Max Of Affine Functions
notes: Read the piecewise-linear graph through active affine functions. Away from a breakpoint one affine piece wins uniquely. At a breakpoint two pieces tie, and the subgradient becomes the convex hull of the active slopes. This is the function analogue of active constraints on a face.

label: Representation Conversion
notes: Explain conversion as a certificate-changing task rather than a cosmetic rewrite. H to V asks for vertices and recession rays; V to H asks for supporting inequalities. Linear images, inverse images, sums, finite maxima, and epigraph constructions preserve polyhedrality because they preserve finite certificates.

label: Numerical H/V Checks
notes: Use the JSON file as an audit trail. Inside samples have nonpositive H-residuals and explicit V-weights plus ray coefficients. The outside sample has a positive residual for the slanted inequality. The piecewise-linear samples confirm that each displayed function value equals the maximum of the affine pieces.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the dictionary. Polyhedral convexity is finite convex geometry: inequalities, generators, faces, cones, epigraphs, and active affine pieces all give mutually checkable certificates. The practical habit is to choose the representation that makes the current question easiest to verify.
